newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian court sentences Albanians to 107 years.
newsitem.headline: Serbian court sentences Albanians to 107 years.

text.p: A court in Serbia's troubled province of Kosovo on Friday sentenced 20 ethnic Albanians charged with hostile activity to a total of 107 years in prison.
The group was charged with the criminal act of association for the purpose of hostile activity, threatening territorial integrity, and terrorism, state news agency Tanjug reported.

Avni Klinaku, the prime defendant, was sentenced to 10 years in prison. He admitted being a member of a clandestine organisation, the National Movement for the Liberation of Kosovo, but denied involvement in terrorism.
The rest of the sentences ranged from two to nine years in prison.
Kosovo, where ethnic Albanians outnumber Serbs nine to one, is widely regarded as a political powder keg which, if ignited, could wreck international peace efforts in the Balkans.

Some 30 people, both Serbs and Albanians, have been killed over the past year in guerrilla violence. Serbian police cracked down on the province in January, arresting some 70 people in a sweep following the guerrilla attacks.
The indictments alleged the defendants wanted to use force to make Kosovo secede from Serbia. The defence denied the charges.
Defence lawyers argued there was no real evidence against the defendants except for confessions during the investigation process, which it alleged were obtained under duress and torture.
Klinaku and co-defendant Shukria Rexha were applauded in the packed courtroom on Tuesday when they announced they were engaged to be married. Rexha was sentenced to three years in prison.

The Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK), the biggest ethnic Albanian party in Kosovo which advocates peaceful resistance to Serb rule, says up to 55 people are still in Serb custody and alleges some have been tortured.

In March, Serbian authorities indicted 15 ethnic Albanians on charges of terrorism, killing three policemen and one Serb civilian, and attempting to murder 16 other people. That group has yet to go on trial.
Serbia revoked Kosovo's autonomy in 1989, claiming its Albanian population wanted to secede and join neighbouring Albania.
The Albanians, led by Ibrahim Rugova, head of the LDK, have boycotted Serbian institutions since but they have been warned by the United States that secession is not an option.
On the other hand, Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic is under pressure to restore human rights in the province if he wants a Washington-imposed "outer wall" of sanctions lifted.
Albanian parties deny the existence of guerrilla groups and say those arrested are victims of Serb persecution.
American intelligence officials believe an ethnic Albanian group, the shadowy Kosovo Liberation Army, has staged at least five armed attacks in the last year.
